hash_scope: SHA-256 of the complete downloaded source bytes (PDF or HTML), before extraction.
extraction_method: PDFs: PyMuPDF/fitz text extraction of every page, with [PDF page N] markers. sources.title: Lecture Notes on Advanced Statistical Theory
sources.author: Ryan Martin
sources.institution: University of Illinois Chicago, Department of Mathematics, Statistics, and Computer Science

actual_reading.anchors: §1.3.5–1.4.2: empirical distribution, parametric families, identifiability, data/model/loss and interpretation.
§2.2–2.3.3: exponential families, factorization/minimal sufficiency, completeness, full-rank theorem, Basu.
Fisher information tail and §2.5 conditional inference examples.
§3.1–3.4: likelihood, MLE, likelihood-ratio asymptotics and their hypotheses/proof.
§5.1–5.7: decision problems, randomization, risk, domination, convex-loss Rao–Blackwellization, Bayes/minimax and constraints.

theorem_hypotheses_and_proof_routes: §2.3.1, Theorem 2.2 states Neyman–Fisher factorization for a common sigma-finite dominating measure and equality mu-a.e.; its proof is explicitly an intuition sketch, with Keener (2010), §6.4 cited for the full proof. That book was not read.
§2.3.2, Theorem 2.3 gives a likelihood-ratio criterion for minimal sufficiency but cites Keener p.47 rather than proving it.

§2.3.3, Theorem 2.6 states completeness for a full-rank d-dimensional exponential family. The proof is only a one-dimensional Laplace-transform sketch; Brown (1986), Theorem 2.12 is cited for the general case and was not read.
§5.2, Theorem 5.1 proves risk reduction by conditional Jensen for a sufficient statistic, convex action set and convex loss; finite risk/integrability should be explicit in a reusable item.
§5.2, Theorem 5.2 says convex loss alone permits removal of randomization, but its averaging proof also needs a convex action set and a finite barycenter. The source omits those hypotheses.
§3.3’s MLE/LR theorems are asymptotic; C1–C4 include fixed support, differentiability/integrability, derivative-interchange and positive information. They are not used as exact inference.
source_limitations_or_defects: §1.4.1, PDF p.23, says the data take values in sample space Theta; context requires X.
Example 2.11, PDF p.39, gives the maximum-uniform density support as 0<t<n; it should be 0<t<theta.
Theorem 2.4 characterization of sufficiency is stated with fixed-support/continuity hypotheses but its proof is omitted and points to Lehmann–Casella.
Theorem 5.2 lacks convex-action and integrability/barycenter hypotheses.

sources.title: Statistical decision problems
sources.author: Peter Hoff
sources.institution: Duke University, Department of Statistical Science

actual_reading.anchors: All sections: inference/estimation setup, randomized tests, loss, decision problem, risk and global criteria.

theorem_hypotheses_and_proof_routes: Pages 2–8 define data/model/estimand, estimator, test function, decision space, loss and expected risk. These are definitions and examples, not theorem proofs.
The preference-representation Theorem 1 on p.10 is malformed in the printed source: both sides compare E under P2, making the displayed equivalence trivial. It is excluded from all claims.
source_limitations_or_defects: Theorem 1, PDF p.10, repeats the P2 expectation on both sides; it cannot support the risk-representation claim as printed.

sources.title: Sufficiency (Mathematical Statistics, Lecture 6)
sources.author: Peter Kempthorne

actual_reading.anchors: Complete focused lecture unit, including sufficiency, factorization proof, reduction in decision risk, minimal sufficiency and likelihood-ratio characterization.

theorem_hypotheses_and_proof_routes: Theorem 1.5.1, pp.8–10, states factorization for a regular model. The proof covers discrete X in both directions, with conditional-mass denominators and zero-support case; p.10 explicitly says advanced absolutely-continuous/general measure proofs are in Ferguson and Lehmann.

Pages 14–15 give a randomized decision-rule construction from the conditional distribution given a sufficient statistic and show equal risk; these slides do not state all measurability/action integrability assumptions.
Pages 17–19 define minimal sufficiency and work the Bernoulli sample-sum reduction; the likelihood-ratio characterization is left as a problem.
source_limitations_or_defects: The factorization proof is only supplied for discrete sample spaces; no general dominated proof is provided in the unit.

sources.title: Sufficiency
sources.author: Will Fithian

actual_reading.anchors: Complete substantive unit: model/statistic/sufficiency definitions, Bernoulli example, factorization statement and discrete proof, normal/Poisson/uniform examples, minimal-sufficiency discussion/proof.

theorem_hypotheses_and_proof_routes: Factorization theorem is stated for common-dominator densities with mu-a.e. equality. The actual proof is expressly limited to discrete X; the reverse direction constructs h(x)=P(X=x|T=T(x)) and uses that it is parameter-free.
Minimal-sufficiency proof is expressly discrete; it uses likelihood-ratio equivalence classes and a measurable reduction argument on each fiber.
source_limitations_or_defects: The HTML includes an interactive visualization with substantial code, not mathematical text; it was retained in extraction but not treated as proof material.

sources.title: Completeness, Ancillarity, and Basu’s Theorem
sources.author: Will Fithian

actual_reading.anchors: Complete substantive unit: completeness definition/examples, full-rank exponential-family theorem and MGF proof, complete-sufficient minimality proof, ancillarity and Basu theorem/proof/example.

theorem_hypotheses_and_proof_routes: §1.3 defines an s-parameter exponential family p_eta(x)=exp{eta'T(x)-A(eta)}h(x), no affine constraint on T, and full rank when the natural-parameter set contains an open set. Theorem states T is complete sufficient.

Proof reduces to canonical T=X and an interior point at zero, uses the zero-expectation identities to equate positive/negative Laplace transforms in a neighborhood, then uniqueness of MGFs. Integrability under the family is implicit and must be stated in an item; the zero-mass case should be dispatched before normalization.
Basu proof uses sufficiency for a parameter-free conditional probability and completeness to show this equals the ancillary marginal probability for every event in a determining class.
source_limitations_or_defects: The page marks itself 'Under construction'; it contains an unrelated placeholder 'Homework 2 Problem XX' and repeats an example number. Do not use those passages.

sources.title: Stat 5421 Lecture Notes: Exponential Families
sources.author: Charles J. Geyer
sources.institution: University of Minnesota, School of Statistics
sources.legal_access: Author-hosted university notes; PDF states CC BY-SA 4.0

actual_reading.anchors: §§3–7: exponential-family/log-likelihood form, full/regular definitions, common support, cumulant derivatives, and identifiability.
§§7.5–11: normal exponential-family form; sufficiency/factorization criterion; IID sufficient dimension reduction and canonical affine reductions.

theorem_hypotheses_and_proof_routes: §3.1 defines the exponential family through log likelihood <y,theta>-c(theta), with parameter-free data terms omitted; §§3.6–3.8 define full/regular and common support/nondegeneracy.

§6 defines identifiability and states the canonical parameter is identifiable iff the canonical statistic is not concentrated on a hyperplane; this equivalently requires a nonsingular variance matrix in a regular full family.
§8.4 states the Neyman–Fisher criterion, but supplies no proof; it asserts the canonical statistic is sufficient by this criterion.
§9.1 directly rewrites the iid log likelihood as a function of the sum of canonical statistics, providing the factorization route for exponential families.
source_limitations_or_defects: No completeness theorem is included in the read units. The factorization criterion itself is asserted rather than proved.

sources.title: STAT 512 Mathematical Statistics Lecture Notes
sources.author: Joshua M. Tebbs
sources.institution: University of South Carolina, Department of Statistics
sources.legal_access: Author-hosted university course notes, copyright by author

actual_reading.anchors: §§7.3–7.4: normal mean/sample variance laws, deferred independence proof, Student t derivation conditional on independence.
§8.4: coverage, pivot definition, quantile inversion, normal-known-variance, exponential, and uniform-maximum examples.
§9.3: conditional definition of sufficiency, Poisson/Rayleigh examples, likelihood, factorization statement, support-dependent uniform/shifted exponential and multi-parameter examples.
§9.4 opening: Rao–Blackwell proof, completeness definition, examples.

theorem_hypotheses_and_proof_routes: §8.4 defines an interval by repeated-sampling coverage and a pivot by parameter-free sampling law. It derives confidence intervals by enclosing the pivot in quantiles and algebraically solving for theta; the proof is event equivalence.

§8.7.1–8.7.2 uses exactly normal iid sampling, known/unknown variance as stated, and chi-square/t sampling laws. The source’s earlier §7.3 explicitly does not prove independence of sample mean and sample variance, so the t interval was excluded as an established result.
§9.3’s Factorization Theorem is stated for an iid sample and discrete/continuous PMF/PDF; no proof is given. Worked examples verify factorization directly.
§9.4 defines completeness through unbiased functions of a sufficient statistic and proves Rao–Blackwell via iterated expectation/variance.
source_limitations_or_defects: §9.3 PDF p.118 prints f(Y|T)=fY/fT as a general continuous implementation; this is not a valid formula for arbitrary lower-dimensional statistics because (Y,T(Y)) is supported on a graph.
The Factorization Theorem statement is not accompanied by proof.
The normal t interval relies on the sample mean/sample variance independence result, which §7.3 explicitly defers.

sources.title: Lecture 10: Confidence intervals
sources.author: Gordan Žitković
sources.edition: Mathematical Statistics, Fall 2017; last updated September 25, 2019

actual_reading.anchors: Complete focused lecture: coverage, pivotal quantities, exact pivot inversion, normal/exponential examples, approximate interval contrast, variance/t intervals, and exercises.

theorem_hypotheses_and_proof_routes: §10.1 defines uniform coverage at least 1-alpha over all parameter values; §10.2 defines a pivot by a parameter-free sampling distribution; §10.3 constructs an interval by quantile calibration followed by event-preserving algebra.
§10.3 warns that scalar inversion is not directly valid for vector-valued parameters; confidence regions require separate treatment.
§10.6 states the normal sample variance/chi-square/t prerequisites but expressly says the full chi-square and mean-variance-independence proofs are beyond scope, supplying only an n=2 illustration.
source_limitations_or_defects: §10.3.2, PDF p.6, prints P[0.44<=U<=1.75]=0.95 although alpha=0.1 and the surrounding lines require 0.9.
The normal sample-variance and t pivots rely on deferred chi-square and independence proofs; not used as established exact results.
